prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle, opening the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the case in this shortlist where a quantitative theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, 2011) was followed years later by an experiment that nobody could have anticipated in detail: correlated insulators and superconductivity in a carbon-only system (2018). It created a tunable platform for strongly correlated electrons, and it has been reproduced by many independent groups using transport, scanning probes and spectroscopy. That is the kind of verified physical discovery, tied to measurement and explained by theory, that I want at the centre of a prize. It also echoes the lesson of graphene itself, where experiment overturned what theorists believed. The three-name configuration is natural: the two authors of the flat-band theory and the leader of the group that made the discovery.
statement.case_against: The origin of the superconductivity and of the correlated phases is still debated, so the field is perhaps a few years short of consolidation, and the discovery is the opening of a field more than a closed physical explanation. The experimental credit is also not clean: Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, and other groups who reproduced and extended the results (for example the Columbia and Harvard groups) are not covered, and a three-person limit forces a hard choice. Topological insulators (B023) are older, better understood and arguably overdue, and the optical lattice clock (B024) is the candidate with the most first-place support and an unambiguous two-person attribution.

responses.point: Ulf ranks B003 first because it is theory leading to a clue found in nature and nature answering, with the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction in 2011 and the Jarillo-Herrero discovery in 2018, while noting that Cao and collaborators are not credited.
responses.response: I agree, and I share the pattern argument; it is the strongest feature of this candidate. I would add that the pattern is only persuasive if the theory was specific, and here it was: the magic angle and the flat-band condition were predicted before the experiment, not fitted afterwards. On Cao, I accept the discomfort. The prize rules limit us to three, and the Cao et al. papers came out of the Jarillo-Herrero group, so I think crediting the group leader is defensible, but I would like us to be explicit in the citation that it is the discovery that is recognised, and not to pretend the credit is complete.

responses.point: Eva ranks the optical lattice clock first and B003 third, observing that the origin of superconductivity and correlated states in twisted graphene is still debated, which makes the interpretation less settled than for the other candidates.
responses.response: That is a fair qualification and I take it seriously, because I ask the same question of robustness. My answer is that the discovery claim and the mechanism claim are separable: the existence of the correlated insulators and the superconducting domes has been independently reproduced in several laboratories and several device geometries, and the continuum model explains the flat bands that underlie them. The Nobel Prize has often preceded a settled mechanism, high-Tc cuprates being the obvious example. Where I differ is on how much weight the unsettled mechanism should carry against the clock's unquestionable maturity; I think it should carry some, which is why I would not oppose B024 as a strong second choice.

responses.point: Stefan puts the optical lattice clock first as a measurement of record precision at the 1e-18 level, independently confirmed by JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, with a clean two-person attribution.
responses.response: I agree that the confirmation and the attribution are the best on the list, and I ranked it seventh mainly because atomic physics is outside my expertise, not because I doubt it. My reservation is one of kind: the clock is a spectacular improvement in a known capability, whereas moire graphene is a new physical regime. Also, Ye's frequency-comb lineage overlaps with the 2005 prize, which some colleagues may see as reducing novelty. If the committee prefers an instrument-driven, unambiguous prize this year, I could support it, and I would like to hear whether you think the redefinition of the second is a necessary condition for timing.

responses.point: Bernhard ranks topological insulators third and B003 fourth, and thinks the moire field is young, so recognition may be premature relative to full understanding of the superconductivity.
responses.response: I accept that B003 is younger than B023 and that I should not hide that. But I find the topological insulator attribution harder than you suggest: Zhang, Bernevig and Hughes made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp tested, and the 3D materials were found by other groups, so a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio leaves out genuine originators, and the 2016 prize already covers topological phases. For moire graphene the theory-plus-discovery trio is closer to complete. I would still put B023 as my first alternative, since its ARPES-verified maturity is a real strength.

uncertainties: Whether the mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene needs to be better established before recognition.
How the committee should treat Yuan Cao and the other experimental groups under a three-person limit.
Whether the 2016 topology prize reduces the room for B023, which would affect how we rank it against B003.
I have not independently verified priority details for the 2018 experiments, and atomic physics (B024) is outside my own expertise.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile; none of the credited names for B003, B023 or B024 is a known collaborator, student or colleague of mine at Uppsala.
